newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian resistance call as PM contender emerges.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian resistance call as PM contender emerges.

text.p: A leader of Cambodia's embattled opposition arrived on the Thai-Cambodian on Tuesday and rallied resistance to strongman Hun Sen nine days after the ouster of First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh. And in the capital Phnom Penh, a confident contender emerged to replace Ranariddh as strongman Hun Sen's coalition partner.

Hun Sen's long-time foe, Sam Rainsy, a former finance minister and ally of Ranariddh, arrived at the Thai border and said he had returned from Europe to help followers who fled after Ranariddh's bloody overthrow on July 6.
A stern critic of Hun Sen, Sam Rainsy said he was joining a resistance with Ranariddh against Hun Sen.
"I told my people to resist as a matter of principle ... to fight against (Second Prime Minister) Hun Sen," he told Reuters in the Thai border town of Aranyaprathet.
"We have agreed to join the resistance with the FUNCINPEC.
"Before I came here I met with Prince Ranariddh and his message to FUNCINPEC is to resist against the dictatorship," he said, referring to Ranariddh's royalist political party.
Sam Rainsy was expelled from the National Assembly in late 1994 after he upset powerful political figures with his campaign against corruption.
Since Ranariddh's overthrow, forces under Hun Sen have pushed troops loyal to the prince back into the jungles of northern Cambodia.
Fighting between troops loyal to the two premiers began in the capital on July 5. The prince had left the country on the eve of the fighting and on July 6 Hun Sen announced Ranariddh's ouster.
Toan Chay, a senior FUNCINPEC member who broke with Ranariddh in April, said on Tuesday he was confident of becoming the prince's replacement as first prime minister.
"I am confident...and even if I lose the premiership I gain in that my people will have peace," he told reporters.
Toan Chay said a senior FUNCINPEC military commander who has been fighting Hun Sen's forces in northern Cambodia was due in Phnom Penh for talks this week.
FUNCINPEC is in dissary in the wake of Ranariddh's overthrow.
Many royalist party members fled from the country after the coup and the killing of at least two senior party officials.
Human rights groups said they were gravely concerned about the safety of hundreds of royalist soldiers and supporters. A diplomatic source said some 25 people had died in custody since the takeover.

The United States has frozen its aid for the moment to Cambodia, and Australia announced on Tuesday it was halting military aid while leaving alone A$32 million (US$23.7 million) a year in general aid.

But major aid donors, while unhappy with the violence, have signalled that they are prepared to live with what has happened so far, as long as peace and freedoms are quickly restored, general elections take place next year and there is no further witchhunt for political foes.

"If Hun Sen crosses those lines the least that will happen is that the aid carpet will be pulled out from under him completely," an authoritative source said in Japan, the biggest aid donor to Cambodia.
Cambodia gets half its annual budget from overseas donations, with Japan by far the biggest contributor.

Indonesia said on Tuesday that foreign ministers from Indonesia, Thailand and the Philippines would meet Ranariddh's father, King Norodom Sihanouk, in Beijing on Thursday to discuss the crisis. Sihanouk has been in the Chinese capital for medical treatment.
